claim: The mushroom body (MB) is the major site of associative odor memory formation in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, the mushroom body (MB) is the major site of associative odor memory formation.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work (Aso et al., 2014a, 2014b) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: 20 types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) each innervate distinct MB compartments.
source: Previously we described the anatomy of the adult MB and defined 20 types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) that each innervate distinct MB compartments (Aso et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: Based on prior published work by the authors (Aso et al., 2014a, 2014b).

claim: Different DAN cell types show extensive differences in training requirements for memory formation.
source: We found extensive differences in training requirements for memory formation, decay dynamics, storage capacity and flexibility to learn new associations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3 comparing different DAN types.

claim: Different DAN cell types show extensive differences in decay dynamics.
source: We found extensive differences in training requirements for memory formation, decay dynamics, storage capacity and flexibility to learn new associations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing memory retention over time.

claim: Different DAN cell types show extensive differences in storage capacity.
source: We found extensive differences in training requirements for memory formation, decay dynamics, storage capacity and flexibility to learn new associations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3F comparing memory capacity.

claim: Different DAN cell types show extensive differences in flexibility to learn new associations.
source: We found extensive differences in training requirements for memory formation, decay dynamics, storage capacity and flexibility to learn new associations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3E testing ability to learn new associations.

claim: A single DAN cell type can either write or reduce an aversive memory, or write an appetitive memory, depending on when it is activated relative to odor delivery.
source: Even a single DAN cell type can either write or reduce an aversive memory, or write an appetitive memory, depending on when it is activated relative to odor delivery.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1F showing ISI curves and Figure 1D showing memory reduction.

claim: Different learning rules are executed in seemingly parallel memory systems.
source: Our results show that different learning rules are executed in seemingly parallel memory systems, providing multiple distinct circuit-based strategies to predict future events from past experiences.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive experimental results showing different properties across compartments.

claim: Individual components of a memory (engrams) are simultaneously stored in distinct sub-circuits whose outputs can be combined upon recall to affect behavior.
source: One idea is that individual components of a memory—often called engrams—are simultaneously stored in distinct sub-circuits whose outputs can then be combined upon recall to affect behavior.
evidence: Presented as a theoretical framework supported by citation (Hikosaka et al., 2014).

claim: Sub-circuits vary in their rules for writing, updating and retaining engrams, having differences in synaptic plasticity and circuit properties.
source: These sub-circuits would vary in their rules for writing, updating and retaining these engrams, having differences in synaptic plasticity and circuit properties (Hikosaka et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation and represents a theoretical framework.

claim: Neuronal circuits for learning associations often share a common architecture where a large array of anatomically similar neurons representing the sensory environment converge onto a much smaller number of output neurons.
source: Neuronal circuits for learning associations often share a common architecture: a large array of anatomically similar neurons that represent the sensory environment converge onto a much smaller number of output neurons (Luo, 2015, Dean et al., 2010) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Punishment or reward activates modulatory neurons that cause changes in the synaptic weight matrix between neurons representing sensory cues and output neurons, resulting in memory formation.
source: Punishment or reward activates modulatory neurons that in turn cause changes in the synaptic weight matrix between the neurons representing the sensory cues and the output neurons, resulting in memory formation.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about learning circuit architecture.

claim: The mushroom body shares the common architecture of learning circuits.
source: The mushroom body (MB) shares this architecture and is the major site of associative learning in Drosophila (Heisenberg et al., 1985; de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2003; Heisenberg, 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Odor identity is represented by a pattern of sparse activity in the ~2000 Kenyon cells (KCs).
source: Odor identity is represented by a pattern of sparse activity in the ~2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994; Perez-Orive et al., 2002), whose parallel axons form the lobes of the MB.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The parallel axons of Kenyon cells form the lobes of the MB.
source: Odor identity is represented by a pattern of sparse activity in the ~2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994; Perez-Orive et al., 2002), whose parallel axons form the lobes of the MB.
evidence: Represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The dendrites of MB output neurons (MBONs) and terminals of dopaminergic input neurons (DANs) tile the KC axons.
source: The dendrites of MB output neurons (MBONs) and terminals of dopaminergic input neurons (DANs) tile the KC axons; the extent of the arbors of individual MBONs and DANs overlap precisely, defining 15 distinct compartmental units that tile the MB lobes of adult Drosophila (Tanaka et al., 2008; Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical work.

claim: The extent of the arbors of individual MBONs and DANs overlap precisely, defining 15 distinct compartmental units that tile the MB lobes of adult Drosophila.
source: The dendrites of MB output neurons (MBONs) and terminals of dopaminergic input neurons (DANs) tile the KC axons; the extent of the arbors of individual MBONs and DANs overlap precisely, defining 15 distinct compartmental units that tile the MB lobes of adult Drosophila (Tanaka et al., 2008; Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical work.

claim: Each compartment contains only one of the three major classes of KCs: γ, α′/β′ and α/β.
source: Each compartment contains only one of the three major classes of KCs: γ, α′/β′ and α/β.
evidence: Represents anatomical knowledge about MB organization.

claim: Each MBON samples from ~90 to ~2000 KCs in one or two compartments.
source: Anatomical data suggest that each MBON samples from ~90 to ~2000 KCs in one or two compartments, while each KC forms en passant synapses on 5–6 types of MBONs along its axon in the lobes (Aso et al., 2009, 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical work.

claim: Each KC forms en passant synapses on 5–6 types of MBONs along its axon in the lobes.
source: Anatomical data suggest that each MBON samples from ~90 to ~2000 KCs in one or two compartments, while each KC forms en passant synapses on 5–6 types of MBONs along its axon in the lobes (Aso et al., 2009, 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical work.

claim: During associative learning, each DAN is thought to modulate KC-MBON synapses only in its target compartment(s).
source: During associative learning, each DAN is thought to modulate KC-MBON synapses only in its target compartment(s) (Hige et al., 2015; Cohn et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work.

claim: The information encoded by KC activity might contribute to multiple distinct engrams by compartmental specific modulation of KC-MBON en passant synapses.
source: Thus, the information encoded by KC activity might contribute to multiple distinct engrams by compartmental specific modulation of KC-MBON en passant synapses.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical and functional data.

claim: KCs, MBONs and DANs innervating individual compartments are differentially involved in forming memories with different valence (appetitive and aversive memories).
source: A large body of previous work has established that the KCs, MBONs and DANs innervating individual compartments are differentially involved in forming memories with different valence—that is, appetitive and aversive memories—and with different stabilities (Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Zars et al., 2000; Isabel et al., 2004; Blum et al., 2009; Krashes et al., 2009; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Aso et al., 2010; Sejourne et al., 2011; Trannoy et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2012; Placais et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2013, Aso et al., 2014b; Lin et al., 2014; Bouzaiane et al., 2015; Ichinose et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to prior work.

claim: KCs, MBONs and DANs innervating individual compartments are differentially involved in forming memories with different stabilities.
source: A large body of previous work has established that the KCs, MBONs and DANs innervating individual compartments are differentially involved in forming memories with different valence—that is, appetitive and aversive memories—and with different stabilities (Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Zars et al., 2000; Isabel et al., 2004; Blum et al., 2009; Krashes et al., 2009; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Aso et al., 2010; Sejourne et al., 2011; Trannoy et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2012; Placais et al., 2013; Pai et al., 2013, Aso et al., 2014b; Lin et al., 2014; Bouzaiane et al., 2015; Ichinose et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to prior work.

claim: Little is known about the rules for writing and updating memory in each compartment.
source: However little is known about the rules for writing and updating memory in each compartment.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Different compartments can employ vastly different learning rules.
source: By using the anatomical map of the MB and cell type specific drivers we reported previously (Aso et al., 2014a, 2014b) in conjunction with newly developed behavioral assays, we have been able to establish that different compartments can employ vastly different learning rules.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Punitive or rewarding stimuli such as electric shock, heat, cold, bitter taste and sugar generally activate a complex pattern of DANs.
source: Punitive or rewarding stimuli such as electric shock, heat, cold, bitter taste and sugar generally activate a complex pattern of DANs (Riemensperger et al., 2005; Mao and Davis, 2009; ; Liu et al., 2012; Tomchik, 2013; Galili et al., 2014; Das et al., 2014; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A reduction in complexity is essential to understand the roles played by DAN inputs to different MB compartments.
source: Believing that a reduction in complexity will be essential to understand the roles played by DAN inputs to different MB compartments, we utilized intersectional split-GAL4 drivers to express CsChrimson, a red-shifted channelrhodopsin, in specific cell types (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Represents the authors' reasoning for their experimental approach.

claim: Pairing one of two odors with activation of PPL1-γ1pedc results in robust aversive memory to the paired odor.
source: Pairing one of two odors with activation of PPL1-γ1pedc, results in robust aversive memory to the paired odor (Aso et al., 2010; Figure 1C–E and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Memory formed by PPL1-γ1pedc activation is fully retained after 10 min.
source: That memory is fully retained after 10 min (blue line in Figure 1D) but has largely decayed by 24 hr (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Memory formed by PPL1-γ1pedc activation has largely decayed by 24 hr.
source: That memory is fully retained after 10 min (blue line in Figure 1D) but has largely decayed by 24 hr (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Presentation of odors alone a few minutes after training resulted in a modest reduction in the conditioned response.
source: Presentation of the odors alone a few minutes after training resulted in a modest reduction in the conditioned response (orange line in Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A second activation of PPL1-γ1pedc a few minutes after training in the absence of odor can almost completely abolish the conditioned response.
source: A second activation of the same DAN a few minutes after training in the absence of odor can almost completely abolish the conditioned response (red line in Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The reduction in conditioned response by unpaired DAN activation most likely results from restoration of the response of the MBON to the odor (erasure of the memory).
source: Recent imaging data of the γ4 MBON (Cohn et al., 2015) suggest that this reduction most likely results from restoration of the response of the MBON to the odor; that is, erasure of the memory.
evidence: Inferred from cited imaging data.

claim: If after the first training, contingencies are reversed such that the other odor is presented paired with DAN activation, the first memory is reduced and a memory of the new association is formed.
source: If, after the first training, contingencies are reversed such that the other odor is presented paired with DAN activation, the first memory is reduced and a memory of the new association is formed (purple line in Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The same DANs can write a new memory or reduce an existing conditioned response, enabling flexibility to rapidly change associations between CS and US.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the same DANs can write a new memory or reduce an existing conditioned response, enabling the flexibility to rapidly change the associations formed between a conditioned stimulus (CS), the odor, and an unconditioned stimulus (US) represented by dopamine release.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: In classical conditioning, both the rate of learning and the valence of the resultant memory depend on the relative timing between the CS and the US.
source: In classical conditioning, both the rate of learning and the valence of the resultant memory depend on the relative timing between the CS and the US (Christian and Thompson, 2003; Gerber et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on classical conditioning.

claim: When PPL1-γ1pedc stimulation falls within a 30-s time window following the onset of a 10-s odor presentation, an aversive memory is formed.
source: We found that when PPL1-γ1pedc stimulation fell within a 30-s time window following the onset of a 10-s odor presentation, an aversive memory was formed (negative PI, Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: DAN stimulation that precedes odor presentation by 20 to 60 s induced an appetitive memory.
source: Interestingly, we observed that DAN stimulation that precedes odor presentation by 20 to 60 s induced an appetitive memory (positive PI, Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: When the timing is such that the CS predicts a subsequent aversive US, animals learn to avoid the CS.
source: These observations are consistent with the notion that it is the predictive aspect of CS-US timing that matters. When the timing is such that the CS predicts a subsequent aversive US, animals learn to avoid the CS.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about classical conditioning.

claim: Animals can learn that the CS predicts the end of an aversive US, and are consequently attracted to the CS.
source: However, animals can also learn that the CS predicts the end of an aversive US, and are consequently attracted to the CS (Tanimoto et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The timing dependency of memory valence could result from the dynamics of the biochemical signaling cascade acting downstream of dopamine receptors.
source: It has been suggested that this timing dependency could result from the dynamics of the biochemical signaling cascade acting downstream of dopamine receptors (Yarali et al., 2012).
evidence: Represents a hypothesis from cited work.

claim: Pairing activation of PPL1-γ1pedc with odor depresses the subsequent spiking rate of the MBON from the γ1pedc compartments in response to the trained odor.
source: Pairing activation of PPL1-γ1pedc with odor has been shown to depresses the subsequent spiking rate of the MBON from the γ1pedc compartments in response to the trained odor (Hige et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior physiological work.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the γ1pedc MBON attracts flies.
source: In behavioral assays, optogenetic activation of this MBON was shown to attract flies (Aso et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior behavioral work.

claim: DAN activation paired with an odor produces an aversive behavioral response to that odor by decreasing the MBON's attractive output.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that DAN activation paired with an odor produces an aversive behavioral response to that odor by decreasing the MBON's attractive output.
evidence: Inferred from combining physiological and behavioral observations.

claim: This single DAN can bi-directionally alter the strength of KC-MBON synapses depending on the presence and relative timing of odor-driven KC activity.
source: Thus our data can be most easily explained if this single DAN can bi-directionally alter the strength of KC-MBON synapses depending on the presence and relative timing of odor-driven KC activity; a full testing of this model awaits additional physiological measurements.
evidence: Represents a hypothesis inferred from the data that requires further testing.

claim: The three DAN cell types that express CsChrimson using the MB320C and MB099C drivers have similar spiking responses to CsChrimson activation.
source: In addition, the three DAN cell types, which express CsChrimson using the MB320C and MB099C drivers, have been shown to have similar spiking responses to CsChrimson activation (Hige et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior physiological work.

claim: In three of six cases, drivers expressing in a combination of two cell types were chosen because activation of only a single DAN cell type did not produce a sufficiently robust memory.
source: In three of six cases, we chose drivers expressing in a combination of two cell types because we found that activation of only a single DAN cell type did not produce a sufficiently robust memory (Figure 2—figure supplements 1,2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The selected drivers showed comparable memory formation when trained with electric shock or sugar reward.
source: We confirmed that the lines used in our optogenetic experiments (Figure 2A) showed comparable memory formation when trained with electric shock or sugar reward (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A 60-s training period resulted in significantly better memory performance compared with a 10-s training for MB043C, MB213B and MB315C+MB109B.
source: A 60-s training period resulted in significantly better memory performance compared with a 10-s training for MB043C, MB213B and MB315C+MB109B (data from ISI = 0 s for MB099C and ISI =+ 10 s for others drivers were used to provide maximum memory formation; see ISI curves in Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Increased learning with 60-s versus 10-s training (PI of 0.72 versus 0.15) was observed when using R58E02-GAL4, a strong GAL4 driver expressed in ~90 PAM cluster DANs.
source: We also observed increased learning with 60-s versus 10-s training (PI of 0.72 versus 0.15) when using R58E02-GAL4 (Liu et al., 2012), a strong GAL4 driver expressed in ~90 PAM cluster DANs that includes all of the ~50 DANs that have expression in MB043C, MB213B and MB315C+MB109B.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation.

claim: Significant aversive 1-day memory was seen with all drivers MB320C, MB099C and MB630B after 10 trainings separated by 15 min resting intervals.
source: Significant aversive 1-day memory was seen with all drivers, while 4-day memory was observed only with MB099C and MB630B.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 4-day memory was observed only with MB099C and MB630B after 10 trainings separated by 15 min resting intervals.
source: Significant aversive 1-day memory was seen with all drivers, while 4-day memory was observed only with MB099C and MB630B.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MB320C failed to show 4-day memory despite displaying the most robust immediate memory.
source: MB320C failed to show 4-day memory despite displaying the most robust immediate memory, while MB630B did not induce significant immediate memory.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MB630B did not induce significant immediate memory.
source: MB320C failed to show 4-day memory despite displaying the most robust immediate memory, while MB630B did not induce significant immediate memory.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Long-term aversive memory in flies requires repetitive electric shock conditioning with resting intervals (spaced training).
source: Long-term aversive memory in flies requires repetitive electric shock conditioning with resting intervals, so-called spaced training (Tully et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Two sets of DANs, PPL1-α3 alone (MB630B) or the combination of PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-α′2α2 (MB099C) can induce 1-day and 4-day aversive memory after spaced training.
source: We found that two sets of DANs, PPL1-α3 alone (MB630B) or the combination of PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-α′2α2 (MB099C) can induce 1-day and 4-day aversive memory after spaced training (Figure 2C), suggesting that the effects of spaced training can be implemented in individual compartments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The effects of spaced training can be implemented in individual compartments.
source: We found that two sets of DANs, PPL1-α3 alone (MB630B) or the combination of PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-α′2α2 (MB099C) can induce 1-day and 4-day aversive memory after spaced training (Figure 2C), suggesting that the effects of spaced training can be implemented in individual compartments.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Making memory formation dependent on repetitive training might be beneficial by allowing an animal to ignore spurious one-time events.
source: Making memory formation dependent on repetitive training might be beneficial by allowing an animal to ignore spurious one-time events.
evidence: Represents a speculative interpretation of the functional significance.

claim: The γ2α′1 compartments play key roles in both sleep regulation and long-term memory.
source: Recent work has shown that the γ2α′1 compartments play key roles in both sleep regulation and long-term memory (Sitaraman et al., 2015; Haynes et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Co-activation of PPL1-γ2α′1 and other DANs synergistically prolongs memory retention.
source: The observation that co-activation of PPL1-γ2α′1 and other DANs synergistically prolongs memory retention (Aso et al., 2012) raises the possibility that PPL1-γ2α′1 might act broadly to facilitate memory consolidation by promoting sleep after learning.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PPL1-γ2α′1 might act broadly to facilitate memory consolidation by promoting sleep after learning.
source: The observation that co-activation of PPL1-γ2α′1 and other DANs synergistically prolongs memory retention (Aso et al., 2012) raises the possibility that PPL1-γ2α′1 might act broadly to facilitate memory consolidation by promoting sleep after learning.
evidence: Represents a speculative hypothesis based on cited observations.

claim: A particular DAN's ability to induce the formation of immediate, 1-day and 4-day memories is not correlated.
source: We found that a particular DAN's ability to induce the formation of immediate, 1-day and 4-day memories is not correlated.
evidence: Inferred from comparing data across different time points in Figure 2C.

claim: Immediate memory after a single pairing with activation of PPL1-α3 (MB630B) was barely detectable, although multiple activations resulted in 4-day memory.
source: For example, immediate memory after a single pairing with activation of PPL1-α3 (MB630B) was barely detectable, although multiple activations resulted in 4-day memory (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc (MB320C) activation resulted in robust immediate memory acquisition after a single round of training, but its activation failed to induce 4-day memory even after extensive spaced training.
source: In contrast, PPL1-γ1pedc (MB320C) activation resulted in robust immediate memory acquisition after a single round of training, but its activation failed to induce 4-day memory even after extensive spaced training (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The stability of memory is an intrinsic property of the MB compartment, rather than a consequence of the training protocol.
source: These results imply the stability of memory is an intrinsic property of the MB compartment, rather than a consequence of the training protocol.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Repetitive training with naturalistic stimuli that activate many DAN cell types would recruit additional compartments with slower acquisition rates.
source: In this view, repetitive training with naturalistic stimuli that activate many DAN cell types would recruit additional compartments with slower acquisition rates and the behaviorally assayed retention of memory would reflect the combined memories formed in different compartments (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Represents a theoretical model based on the data.

claim: The behaviorally assayed retention of memory would reflect the combined memories formed in different compartments.
source: In this view, repetitive training with naturalistic stimuli that activate many DAN cell types would recruit additional compartments with slower acquisition rates and the behaviorally assayed retention of memory would reflect the combined memories formed in different compartments (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Represents a theoretical model based on the data.

claim: The data are consistent with a model in which memory formation and consolidation can occur independently and in parallel in individual MB compartments.
source: For olfactory learning in Drosophila, our data are consistent with a model in which memory formation and consolidation can occur independently and in parallel in individual MB compartments; this view does not exclude the possibility that network activity facilitates memory consolidation.
evidence: Represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: The memories induced in different compartments have different stabilities, displaying different dynamics of spontaneous memory decay over a 1-day period.
source: We found that the memories induced in different compartments have different stabilities, displaying different dynamics of spontaneous memory decay over a 1-day period (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Memories in each compartment differed in the extent to which they were reduced by a second presentation of the trained odor without reinforcement.
source: Memories in each compartment also differed in the extent to which they were reduced by a second presentation of the trained odor without reinforcement (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DAN activation without odor presentation significantly reduced immediate memory for four of the five sets of DANs tested.
source: Likewise, DAN activation without odor presentation significantly reduced immediate memory (Figure 3D) for four of the five sets of DANs tested.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The effects of odor presentation alone and dopamine without odor might be mechanistically linked as odor presentation alone can result in activation of a subset of dopaminergic neurons.
source: These two effects might be mechanistically linked as odor presentation alone can result in activation of a subset of dopaminergic neurons (Riemensperger et al., 2005; Mao and Davis, 2009).
evidence: Represents a hypothesis based on cited observations.

claim: It would make sense for a memory to be diminished when the contingency upon which it is based is found to be unreliable.
source: In both the case of presentation of odor without dopamine and of dopamine without odor, the association the fly had previously learned is not confirmed. It would make sense for a memory to be diminished when the contingency upon which it is based is found to be unreliable.
evidence: Represents a functional interpretation of the observations.

claim: Repetitive spaced training with MB099C or MB630B can induce 1-day memory that is resistant to DAN activation.
source: Consistent with this idea, repetitive spaced training with these same DANs can induce 1-day memory that is resistant to DAN activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different compartments weigh the importance of the reliability of the correlation between CS and US differently.
source: The differences we observed between compartments suggest that they weigh the importance of the reliability of the correlation between CS and US differently.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The α1 compartment was resistant to memory reduction by DAN activation.
source: The α1 compartment differed from the other compartments we tested in that it was resistant to memory reduction by DAN activation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The α1 compartment plays a key role in long-term appetitive memory of nutritious foods.
source: This compartment plays a key role in long-term appetitive memory of nutritious foods (Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015) and has an unusual circuit structure: its MBON (MBON-α1) appears to form synapses on the dendrites of the DAN that innervates the α1 compartment (PAM-α1) forming a recurrent circuit necessary for long-term memory formation (Ichinose et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The α1 compartment has an unusual circuit structure where its MBON (MBON-α1) appears to form synapses on the dendrites of the DAN that innervates the α1 compartment (PAM-α1) forming a recurrent circuit necessary for long-term memory formation.
source: This compartment plays a key role in long-term appetitive memory of nutritious foods (Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015) and has an unusual circuit structure: its MBON (MBON-α1) appears to form synapses on the dendrites of the DAN that innervates the α1 compartment (PAM-α1) forming a recurrent circuit necessary for long-term memory formation (Ichinose et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The α1 compartment showed the least ability to replace an older association with a new one.
source: The α1 compartment also showed the least ability to replace an older association with a new one (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The initial memory in the α1 compartment may not be affected by the second training, resulting in co-existing appetitive memories for both odors.
source: This observation suggests that the initial memory may not be affected by the second training, resulting in co-existing appetitive memories for both odors.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Flies were able to retain associations between each of two odors and PAM-α1 (MB043C) activation.
source: Indeed, flies were able to retain associations between each of two odors and PAM-α1 (MB043C) activation, while only the most recently learned association was remembered with PPL1-γ1pedc (MB320C) activation (3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Only the most recently learned association was remembered with PPL1-γ1pedc (MB320C) activation.
source: Indeed, flies were able to retain associations between each of two odors and PAM-α1 (MB043C) activation, while only the most recently learned association was remembered with PPL1-γ1pedc (MB320C) activation (3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The higher memory capacity of the α1 compartment is not due to generalization, since training with one odor pair did not affect the innate odor preference observed with a different, untrained odor pair.
source: The higher memory capacity of the α1 compartment is not due to generalization, since training with one odor pair did not affect the innate odor preference observed with a different, untrained odor pair.
evidence: Inferred from experimental controls.

claim: Two distinct strategies for updating memories are used in different MB compartments: (1) writing a new memory, while diminishing the old memory; or (2) writing a new memory, while retaining the old memory.
source: Thus two distinct strategies for updating memories appear to be used in different MB compartments: (1) writing a new memory, while diminishing the old memory; or (2) writing a new memory, while retaining the old memory.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Memory formation in each compartment is largely parallel and independent, with compartmental specific rules for updating memories.
source: Our results suggest that memory formation in each compartment is largely parallel and independent, with compartmental specific rules for updating memories.
evidence: Represents an interpretation of the overall results.

claim: A model of independent memory storage should allow appetitive and aversive memories to be simultaneously formed for the same odor in different compartments.
source: Such a model of independent memory storage should allow appetitive and aversive memories to be simultaneously formed for the same odor in different compartments.
evidence: Represents a prediction from the model.

claim: When flies were tested immediately after simultaneous activation of DANs to α1 and γ1pedc while exposing flies to an odor, the odor was strongly aversive, but the same odor became appetitive after 1 day.
source: We tested this idea by simultaneously activating DANs to α1 and γ1pedc while exposing flies to an odor (Figure 4A). When flies were tested immediately after training, the odor was strongly aversive, but the same odor became appetitive after 1 day.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The shift in valence over time is most easily explained by simultaneous formation of an aversive memory in γ1pedc and an appetitive memory in α1, with rapid decay of the memory in γ1pedc and slow decay in α1.
source: These results are most easily explained by simultaneous formation of an aversive memory in γ1pedc and an appetitive memory in α1, with rapid decay of the memory in γ1pedc and slow decay in α1 resulting in a shift in valence of the conditioned response over time.
evidence: Represents an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The observation of strongly aversive immediate memory, rather than an intermediate response, suggests that the MB network non-linearly integrates conflicting signals.
source: However, the fact that we observed strongly aversive immediate memory, rather than an intermediate response, suggests that the MB network non-linearly integrates these conflicting signals.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The known feedforward connection between γ1pedc and α1 provides a possible circuit mechanism for non-linear integration.
source: The known feedforward connection between γ1pedc and α1 provides a possible circuit mechanism (Figure 5B; Aso et al. 2014a).
evidence: Based on prior anatomical knowledge and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Wild type flies are capable of efficiently switching odor preference when they had conflicting sequential experiences of sugar reward followed by shock punishment with the same odor.
source: We also found that wild type flies are capable of efficiently switching odor preference when they had conflicting sequential experiences of sugar reward followed by shock punishment with the same odor (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Different MB compartments use distinct rules for writing and updating memories of odors.
source: Our results demonstrate that different MB compartments use distinct rules for writing and updating memories of odors (Figure 5A).
evidence: Represents the main conclusion supported by all experimental data.

claim: The interpretation of a common odor representation carried by sparse KC activity to multiple compartments could be modified differently in each of those compartments.
source: By analyzing individual memory components–or engrams–induced by local dopamine release, we found that the interpretation of a common odor representation carried by sparse KC activity to multiple compartments could be modified differently in each of those compartments.
evidence: Represents an interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: The distinct learning rules could arise from differences in the dopamine release properties of different DAN cell types.
source: We do not know the mechanisms that generate these distinct learning rules. They could arise from differences in the dopamine release properties of different DAN cell types or from local differences in the biochemical response to dopamine signaling in each MB compartment.
evidence: Represents a speculative hypothesis about mechanisms.

claim: The distinct learning rules could arise from local differences in the biochemical response to dopamine signaling in each MB compartment.
source: We do not know the mechanisms that generate these distinct learning rules. They could arise from differences in the dopamine release properties of different DAN cell types or from local differences in the biochemical response to dopamine signaling in each MB compartment.
evidence: Represents a speculative hypothesis about mechanisms.

claim: KCs express four distinct dopamine receptors, which might be deployed differently in each compartment.
source: For example, KCs express four distinct dopamine receptors (Crocker et al., 2016), which might be deployed differently in each compartment.
evidence: Based on cited work and represents a speculative hypothesis.

claim: The distinct learning rules could originate from circuit properties, as MB compartments can communicate through connections between their extrinsic neurons.
source: Or they could originate from circuit properties: we know from anatomical (Tanaka et al., 2008; Aso et al., 2014a), behavioral (Ichinose et al., 2015) and functional imaging (Boto et al., 2014; Cohn et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015) studies that MB compartments can communicate through connections between their extrinsic neurons, the DANs and MBONs, as well as by a layered network within the MB (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and represents a hypothesis.

claim: In the mammalian brain, associative memories are also stored as distributed and parallel changes with partially overlapping functions.
source: In the mammalian brain, associative memories are also stored as distributed and parallel changes with partially overlapping functions (Herry and Johansen, 2014; Hikosaka et al., 2014; Tonegawa et al., 2015); for example, different populations of dopaminergic neurons develop representations of a visual objects' value with distinct learning rules (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to work in mammalian systems.

claim: Different populations of dopaminergic neurons in mammals develop representations of a visual object's value with distinct learning rules.
source: In the mammalian brain, associative memories are also stored as distributed and parallel changes with partially overlapping functions (Herry and Johansen, 2014; Hikosaka et al., 2014; Tonegawa et al., 2015); for example, different populations of dopaminergic neurons develop representations of a visual objects' value with distinct learning rules (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to work in mammalian systems.

claim: Many of the underlying strategies and mechanisms may be shared between flies and other species.
source: We expect many of the underlying strategies and mechanisms may be shared between flies and other species.
evidence: Represents a speculative prediction based on comparative considerations.

claim: This work provides a foundation for experiments aimed at understanding the molecular and circuit mechanisms by which distributed memory components are written with distinct rules and later integrated to guide memory-based behaviors.
source: Our work provides a foundation for experiments aimed at understanding the molecular and circuit mechanisms by which distributed memory components are written with distinct rules and later integrated to guide memory-based behaviors.
evidence: Represents a statement about the significance of the work.

claim: Dopamine signaling to KCs has been implicated in both learning and forgetting.
source: Dopamine signaling to KCs has been implicated in both learning and forgetting (Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Schroll et al., 2006, Kim et al., 2007; Tomchik and Davis, 2009; Gervasi et al., 2010; Qin et al., 2012; Placais et al., 2012; Berry et al., 2012; Boto et al., 2014; Shuai et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Control genotypes did not show any significant memory in the same training protocols.
source: Control genotypes did not show any significant memory in the same training protocols: (1) no driver control, pBDPGAL4 in attP2/20xUAS-CsChrimson in attP18 (PI = 0.07, SEM = 0.037, N = 14); and (2) no effector control, MB320C/w1118 (PI = −0.01, SEM = 0.031, N = 10).
evidence: Supported by experimental control data.

claim: For appetitive memory, the period when dopamine signaling resulted in the most robust memory formation was shifted slightly later relative to odor presentation.
source: Thus, for appetitive memory, the period when dopamine signaling resulted in the most robust memory formation was shifted slightly later relative to odor presentation; such a response profile might be an adaptation to the time required for converting ingested food to a nutritional reward signal.
evidence: Inferred from ISI curve data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Individual MB compartments can be modeled as distinct memory units with different baseline acquisition rates and memory stabilities, which can be set independently.
source: Based on this and previous studies (Hige et al., 2015; Aso et al., 2012), we propose that to a first approximation individual MB compartments can be modeled as distinct memory units with different baseline acquisition rates and memory stabilities, which can be set independently.
evidence: Represents a theoretical model based on current and prior data.

claim: For aversive memory, memory stability and acquisition rate appear negatively correlated.
source: For aversive memory, we found memory stability and acquisition rate appear negatively correlated (Figure 2 and Figure 3B).
evidence: Inferred from comparing data in Figures 2 and 3B.

claim: Stable appetitive memory can be induced by brief training.
source: However, stable appetitive memory can be induced by brief training (Figure 3B) (Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3B and citations.

claim: Activating the combined drivers MB315C+MB109B induced significantly higher appetitive memory than obtained by activating either driver alone.
source: Activating the combined drivers induced significantly higher appetitive memory than obtained by activating either driver alone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Training ten times with 15-min rest intervals (10x spaced training) resulted in significant 4-day aversive memory when using the three drivers, MB099C, MB060B and MB065B that express in the combination of the γ2, α′1, α′2 and α2 compartments.
source: Training ten times with 15-min rest intervals (10x spaced training) resulted in significant 4-day aversive memory when using the three drivers, MB099C, MB060B and MB065B that express in the combination of the γ2, α′1, α′2 and α2 compartments (PPL1-γ2α′1 and PPL1-α′2α2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Drivers expressing either in just α′2 plus α2 (MB058B) or just in γ2 plus α′1 (MB296B), failed to induce 4-day memory.
source: Drivers expressing either in just α′2 plus α2 (MB058B) or just in γ2 plus α′1 (MB296B), failed to induce 4-day memory.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MB296B expresses in PPL1-γ2α′1, a subset of the expression pattern of MB099C.
source: MB296B expresses in PPL1-γ2α′1, a subset of the expression pattern of MB099C, and MB063B expresses in PAM-β1, a subset of the expression pattern of MB213B (Aso et al. 2014a).
evidence: Based on prior anatomical characterization.

claim: MB063B expresses in PAM-β1, a subset of the expression pattern of MB213B.
source: MB296B expresses in PPL1-γ2α′1, a subset of the expression pattern of MB099C, and MB063B expresses in PAM-β1, a subset of the expression pattern of MB213B (Aso et al. 2014a).
evidence: Based on prior anatomical characterization.

claim: MB296B and MB063B show significant memory compared to the control genotype, but much weaker than the combination lines (MB099C and MB213B).
source: These drivers show significant memory compared to the control genotype, but much weaker than the combination lines (MB099C and MB213B; see Figure 2B) used in our main experiments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: All split-GAL4 lines tested show roughly similar levels of memory formation with naturalistic stimuli (shock or sugar), indicating that the failure to form some types of memory by optogenetic stimulation of a specific DAN is unlikely to be due to differences in genetic background between lines.
source: The results show that all lines show roughly similar levels of memory formation, indicating that the failure to form some types of memory by optogenetic stimulation of a specific DAN is unlikely to be due to differences in genetic background between lines.
evidence: Inferred from control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: MB099C showed significant aversive memory only at ISI = 0 s.
source: MB099C showed significant aversive memory only at ISI = 0 s; ISI = −10 s and +10 s were significant without correction for multiple comparisons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: MB043C, MB213B and MB315C+MB109B all showed significant appetitive memory at ISI = +10 s and +30 s.
source: MB043C, MB213B and MB315C+MB109B all showed significant appetitive memory at ISI = +10 s and +30 s; MB315C+MB109B also showed significant appetitive memory at ISI = 0.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: MB315C+MB109B showed significant appetitive memory at ISI = 0.
source: MB043C, MB213B and MB315C+MB109B all showed significant appetitive memory at ISI = +10 s and +30 s; MB315C+MB109B also showed significant appetitive memory at ISI = 0.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Memory induced by spaced training with MB099C or MB630B and tested after 1 d does not show a significant reduction after DAN activation.
source: Unlike with immediate memory that was induced by a single training (Figure 3D), memory induced by spaced training with MB099C or MB630B and tested after 1 d does not show a significant reduction after DAN activation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: When flies expressing CsChrimson in both PPL1-γ1pedc and PAM-α1 were trained and tested immediately, the odor was strongly aversive.
source: Flies expressing CsChrimson in PPL1-γ1pedc (VT045661-LexA in JK22C x 13xLexAop2-CsChrimson-tdTomato in attP18), or in PAM-α1 (MB043C x 20xUAS-CsChrimson-mVenus in attP18), or in both PPL1-γ1pedc and PAM-α1 (by combining all four transgenes) were starved for 48 hr and then trained with a 60-s odor delivery during which thirty 1-s pulses of red light were given, and then tested either immediately or after 1 d.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When flies expressing CsChrimson in both PPL1-γ1pedc and PAM-α1 were trained and tested after 1 day, the odor became appetitive.
source: Flies expressing CsChrimson in PPL1-γ1pedc (VT045661-LexA in JK22C x 13xLexAop2-CsChrimson-tdTomato in attP18), or in PAM-α1 (MB043C x 20xUAS-CsChrimson-mVenus in attP18), or in both PPL1-γ1pedc and PAM-α1 (by combining all four transgenes) were starved for 48 hr and then trained with a 60-s odor delivery during which thirty 1-s pulses of red light were given, and then tested either immediately or after 1 d.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wild type flies were trained using 2-min exposures to odor A with sucrose and then to odor B without sucrose and tested for odor preference after 1d, showing appetitive memory.
source: Wild type flies were starved for 48 hr and then trained using 2-min exposures to odor A with sucrose and then to odor B without sucrose and tested for odor preference after 1d (Test 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Following appetitive training, flies were trained with a 1-min exposure of odor A (the odor previously paired with sugar) and electric shock and then with odor B without shock, and odor preference was measured immediately after the second training, showing aversive memory.
source: Following the first memory test, flies were trained with a 1-min exposure of odor A (the odor previously paired with sugar) and electric shock (twelve 1.25 s pulses of 60V) in the olfactory arena and then with odor B without shock. Odor preference was measured immediately after the second training (Test 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.
